clue.text: No hope with cards dealt in game

indicators.note: cards that are dealt get mixed and handed out in a fresh order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A card player holding a hopeless hand in some game.
explanation.walkthrough: SANCHO PEDRO is an old American card game; the card-table surface keeps you thinking of the hand rather than of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sancho Pedro is a trick-taking card game related to pitch, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: Habitual drinker holding nose in need of treatment urgently

indicators.note: something in need of treatment is out of order, so these letters must be set right in a new arrangement
holding means one piece clasps the other inside it

blocks.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard
taken as written

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker with a damaged nose needing urgent medical attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treatment urgently' reads as a single phrase, but 'urgently' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Soonest, as in 'the sooner the better', is an adverb meaning at the earliest possible time, which is to act urgently.

clue.text: A garment for a man, horrible thing Trish put out

indicators.note: something horrible has been mangled out of shape, so its letters are reworked
put out means upset or disturbed, so these letters are disturbed into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Trish is offended by a hideous item of clothing bought for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightshirt is a long shirt worn in bed, traditionally by men, so it is a male garment.

clue.text: For this reason, strengthen ceiling, in part

indicators.note: in part says only a portion of the run of words is wanted, sitting inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A builder justifying reinforcement work on a ceiling.
explanation.definitionFit: Hence is a formal adverb meaning therefore, as a result of what was just said.

clue.text: A fruit pie - pen pal, out of shape, tucked in

indicators.note: out of shape means bent from its proper form, so these letters are reformed
tucked in means placed snugly inside something else

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A misshapen correspondent tucking into a fruit pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A fruit pie' looks like one item, but 'A fruit' is the definition and the pie is the outer shell of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The pineapple is a tropical fruit with spiky skin and sweet yellow flesh.

clue.text: Accomplished daughter, single

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
single means one

explanation.surface: Describing a talented daughter who is not married.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accomplished' looks like an adjective praising the daughter; here it is a past participle meaning finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accomplished has been completed, i.e. it is finished and over with.

clue.text: Bird, variegated sort, one on top of church

indicators.note: variegated means mixed in colour or pattern, so these letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
CH is the usual abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A multicoloured kind of bird perched on a church roof.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on top of' puts the numeral above the church abbreviation, i.e. before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ostrich is a large flightless African bird, the biggest living species.

clue.text: The sort of wedding the bride must be expecting to have

definitions.text: The sort of wedding the bride must be expecting to have

blocks.note: surface reading: a style of ceremony the bride has been anticipating
setter's reading: expecting means pregnant, forcing a hurried marriage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Expecting' looks like 'anticipating' but means pregnant: a wedding hastily arranged because of a pregnancy, traditionally under threat from the bride's father's gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A shotgun wedding is an idiom for a marriage forced on the couple because the bride is pregnant.

clue.text: Inferior type of stamp

blocks.note: first meaning: of lower quality or status
second meaning: the cheaper, slower postage stamp in the UK

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one description of a poor stamp. British post has first-class and cheaper, slower second-class stamps.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-class means of lesser standing, and a second-class stamp pays for the slower UK postal service.

clue.text: An indefinite number on street work around the clock

blocks.note: in maths n stands for an unspecified number
taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for street
OP, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: Unspecified numbers of people working shifts on a street at all hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonstop means continuous without a break, the same as round-the-clock activity.

clue.text: Salute current members

blocks.note: current means present, of now
arms are limbs, i.e. members of the body

explanation.surface: Greeting the people who currently belong to a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' suggests club membership, but it is used in its old sense of limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Present arms is a military salute in which the rifle is held upright in front of the body.

clue.text: Have a leisurely conversation with that chef we trained

indicators.note: trained means drilled into a new form, so these letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Chatting idly with a chef the speaker has trained.
explanation.definitionFit: Chew the fat is an informal idiom for chatting at length in a relaxed way.

clue.text: English TV channel

blocks.note: first meaning: spin put on a ball in billiards or snooker
second meaning: an informal British word for a broadcast channel

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a British broadcaster. In American pool, English is spin on the cue ball, which the British call side; Britons also used to ask what was on 'the other side'.
explanation.definitionFit: Side is the British billiards term for spin, called English in the US, and an informal word for a television channel.

clue.text: Citrus fruit, kind that is found around the North

indicators.note: found around means sitting so as to enclose something else

blocks.note: clement means merciful, kind
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
N is the abbreviation for North

explanation.surface: A variety of citrus fruit that grows in northern regions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' looks like a noun meaning variety, but it is the adjective meaning merciful.
explanation.definitionFit: A clementine is a small seedless citrus fruit, a hybrid of the mandarin and sweet orange.

clue.text: Nick, bridge player, disheartened holding clubs

indicators.note: disheartened means having lost its heart, so the central letter is removed
holding means one piece grips the other inside it

blocks.note: the four bridge players are named by compass points
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card notation

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick at the bridge table, downcast while holding clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a player's name; it is the definition, a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A notch is a small V-shaped cut, the same as a nick in an edge.

clue.text: Cheers up, in a way, absorbing Latin in vault

indicators.note: in a way suggests the letters are set out after some fashion of their own, rearranged
absorbing means taking something inside itself

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: Someone cheering up by studying Latin in a cellar.
explanation.definitionFit: A sepulchre is a stone tomb or burial chamber, a vault for the dead.

clue.text: Secretary's initial answer's to get rid of raised typeface

indicators.note: initial points to the opening letter of the word before it
in a down clue, raised means lifted up the column, so the word is read bottom to top

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
ANS is the usual abbreviation for answer, plus the 's
to fire is to dismiss, get rid of

explanation.surface: A secretary's first idea is to ditch a fancy raised font.
explanation.definitionFit: Sans serif is a style of typeface whose letters lack the small strokes, called serifs, at their ends.

clue.text: The thumbs up for demolition

blocks.note: first meaning: official permission to proceed
second meaning: the removal of buildings

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as approval being given for demolition work; the single word means both the approval and the knocking-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Clearance is authorisation to go ahead, and also the clearing away of old buildings from a site.

clue.text: Decent chalet, I suspect

indicators.note: suspect means dubious or unsound, so the letters are not to be trusted in their given order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone judging a chalet acceptable, though only as a guess.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethical means morally right, which is what decent behaviour is.

clue.text: A myth? Awful nonsense!

indicators.note: awful means dreadful or botched, so the letters come out in a muddled order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone scoffing at a myth as dreadful rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful nonsense' reads as one phrase, but 'Awful' is the signal and 'nonsense!' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: My hat! is a dated British exclamation of disbelief, used like saying rubbish or nonsense.

clue.text: To be busily active on house is commonplace

blocks.note: a place that hums is buzzing with activity
drum is slang for a house or home

explanation.surface: Keeping busy around the house is ordinary routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Drum is British slang for a house or flat. In a down clue, 'on' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Humdrum describes something dull and routine, lacking excitement, which is what commonplace means.

clue.text: A continuous pain? One must ring hospital

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: an ace counts as one in cards and dice
H is the abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Someone in constant pain told to phone the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests a phone call; here it means surround.
explanation.definitionFit: An ache is a dull, persistent pain, as opposed to a sharp momentary one.

clue.text: Shooting star and new moon observed by extremely eager scientist

indicators.note: shooting suggests something flying apart, so these letters are scattered into a new order
new means made afresh, so these letters are remade in a different order
extremely points to the extremes, the two end letters of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A keen scientist watching a shooting star and a new moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shooting star' and 'new moon' look like fixed phrases, but each first word is a separate signal acting on the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronomer is a scientist who studies stars, planets and other celestial bodies.

clue.text: Reportedly studies marsh plants

indicators.note: reportedly means as told by word of mouth, so it is the sound that counts

blocks.note: to read a subject is to study it

explanation.surface: Word goes round that someone is researching wetland vegetation.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage to read a subject is to study it at university.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeds are tall grasses that grow in marshes and shallow water.

clue.text: Money from an Orton play

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for cash
second meaning: the 1965 black comedy by Joe Orton

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as box-office takings from a play. Joe Orton was an English playwright of dark farces.
explanation.definitionFit: Loot is informal slang for money, and is the title of a farce by the dramatist Joe Orton.

clue.text: A helping hand given by gullible type, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word is caught by ear, so only its sound matters

blocks.note: a sucker is someone easily fooled

explanation.surface: Help offered by a naive person, so people say.
explanation.definitionFit: Succour is assistance and support given in a time of need, a helping hand.

clue.text: Boat people perhaps see grim changes

indicators.note: changes means alters, so these letters are put into another arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Refugees at sea witness grim upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks the definition as an example: boat people are one kind of emigrant.
explanation.definitionFit: Emigrés are people who have left their country, often for political reasons, as boat people did fleeing by sea.

clue.text: Reprieved, second eleven released pent-up emotions

blocks.note: to be let off is to be spared punishment
S is the abbreviation for second
a cricket or football team has eleven players

explanation.surface: A reserve football side, spared relegation, lets their feelings out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second eleven' reads as a reserve team; it splits into an abbreviation and a team.
explanation.definitionFit: To let off steam is an idiom for releasing stored-up energy or anger, like a boiler venting pressure.
